title: The centurion's faith (Luke 7:1–10)
hook: a Roman officer says: just say the word

segments.voice: Yesterday, blind guides, a beam in the eye, and a storehouse in the heart. Your line was out of the heart the mouth speaks. What came out of your storehouse yesterday? Day five hundred twenty-six.
screen: `OUT OF THE HEART THE MOUTH SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: A centurion was a military officer, and this one is not Jewish. An unlikely person at the center of a story about faith in a small Jewish town. But in Capernaum, Luke says, there's a centurion whose servant is dying, a servant "who was dear unto him." And here's the first surprise: the centurion doesn't go to Jesus himself. He sends the elders of the Jewish community to ask for him. And they come and plead his case warmly. He's worthy, they say: "For he loveth our nation, and he hath built us a synagogue." A foreign officer, and the town's elders are his advocates.
screen: `THE ELDERS: HE BUILT US A SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: So Jesus goes with them. And when he's nearly at the house, the centurion sends friends with a message. In the King James words: "Lord, trouble not thyself: for I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof." Notice what's going on. The elders said he's worthy. He says I'm not worthy. A man who gives orders to soldiers, telling a traveling teacher from Nazareth, don't trouble yourself with me. And then he explains why he doesn't need Jesus to come at all: "say in a word, and my servant shall be healed. For I also am a man set under authority, having under me soldiers, and I say unto one, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh." He understands orders. He knows a word from the right person is enough, no matter the distance. He doesn't need to see a touch or a gesture. Just the word. Luke says Jesus "marvelled at him." This time Jesus is the one amazed. Jesus turns to the crowd and says: "I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel." And when the friends get back to the house, the servant is well. In Luke's version, the centurion and Jesus never meet face to face. The whole story happens through messengers, and through a word sent across a distance. Catholics echo the centurion at Mass: just before communion, the people say they are not worthy for the Lord to come under their roof, but ask him only to say the word. An officer's message, still spoken in churches today.
screen: `A MAN UNDER AUTHORITY: SAY THE WORD.`
then, large: `SAY IN A WORD, AND MY SERVANT SHALL BE HEALED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send a word across a distance. Settle, and breathe. The centurion never stood in the room; his message traveled for him. Bring to mind someone you can't easily reach right now: a friend in another city, a relative you rarely see, someone in a hospital bed or a hard season. Picture where they are at this moment. Now find the word you'd send them, short enough to fit in one breath. Thinking of you. I haven't forgotten. I'm here. Say it slowly in your mind, as if it were already on its way. If you pray, you can echo the centurion and ask God only to say the word for them. If you don't, simply hold the word and the person together. The bell holds the time.
The centurion's faith. A Roman officer who says he isn't worthy to have Jesus under his roof, and trusts that one word, sent from a distance, is enough.
Your line: only say the word. Send one kind word to someone today, a text or a note, and trust that it can do its work from a distance. Day five hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: At Catholic Mass, just before communion, the congregation says a form of the centurion's words, saying they are not worthy for the Lord to enter under their roof and asking him only to say the word.

fork.setup: you're a Roman officer. the teacher you asked for is almost at your door. what do you do?
options: meet him at the gate with honor.
send friends: don't trouble yourself; only say the word.
send soldiers to hurry him along.
fork.reveal: the centurion sends word that he isn't worthy to have Jesus under his roof, and that a word is enough. Jesus marvels at his faith.

original.note: Greek: commander of a hundred, a centurion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a soldier asks for a healing.
what it means: an outsider, vouched for by the town's elders, believes a word from Jesus can heal across a distance, and Jesus marvels.
what a scholar hears: in Luke the two never meet, while in Matthew the centurion comes himself; the whole story turns on a sent word.

notes: The Mass response is described, not quoted (the current English wording is copyrighted).
'Still spoken in churches around the world' refers to the Mass response. Confirm.
'Marvelled' (thaumazo) applied to Jesus is rare in the Gospels (also Mark 6:6). Confirm 'almost never'.
Greek hekatontarches spelling in Luke 7:2 (Luke uses hekatontarches). Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): rewrote the practice, which repeated day 519's 'let a kindness land' exercise, so it now fits the carry (a word sent across a distance); cut 'around a hundred soldiers' (twice), 'which almost never happens in the Gospels' and 'at every Mass'; 'Roman officer' softened to a non-Jewish officer, since Luke does not say whom he served (possibly Herod Antipas's forces).
